title: Instance profiles and IRSA: credentials without a static key

videos.script: A key written into a program is a key somebody will find. This lesson is about programs that carry none at all. {{chain}} Every AWS tool looks for credentials in a fixed order. It tries the environment first, then the files in your home directory, then a list of other places. The first place that answers wins. {{bottom}} At the bottom of that list are places the platform fills in for you. On EC2, the machine asks a small service at a fixed address. {{imds}} That service answers with credentials for the machine's role, and replaces them before they expire. Nobody copies a key onto the disk. {{ssrf}} The same service is a target. An application tricked into fetching that address hands its role to a stranger, and you will see the settings that close that door. {{pods}} A cluster needs more than one role per machine. On EKS, each pod gets a signed token, and trades it for a role of its own. {{moto}} You will run every step against moto, and measure what it checks. The answer is surprising, and it tells you which half of this lesson to trust from AWS's documentation instead. {{end}}
